source: Bossard et al. (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: advances in the RPD model
finding: Opinion piece. RPD has three levels: simple match, diagnosis, evaluation by mental simulation. It lists qualitative RPD studies in about a dozen sports (badminton, volleyball, soccer, ice hockey, handball, basketball, judo, karate, rugby coaches, adventure coaches, officials).
numbers: Lists about 20 studies; all qualitative interview or self-confrontation designs.
quote: Experts use their experiences to focus their perceptions onto salient features, to recognize situations as typical, and to choose the most appropriate option.
limits: Opinion article, not a systematic count. Support is mostly interview-based and retrospective.
agent_relevance: Agent scaffold: recognise typicality first, then pick the first adequate option. Sport shows this is the common mode, not the only one.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: advances in the RPD model (usage rates)
finding: Citing Macquet (2020): in sport, most expert decisions are simple matches, some diagnosis, few evaluation by simulation. Time pressure is the stated reason for the dominance of intuition.
numbers: Simple match 60-81%; diagnosis 13-28%; evaluation 3-24% of expert decisions.
limits: Ranges are wide because sports, roles and coding schemes differ. Macquet (2020) itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives a prior for how often a fast path should suffice: roughly two thirds to four fifths. Evaluation by simulation should be the rare, triggered path.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: advances in the RPD model (time and role)
finding: Boundary condition: when athletes were far from the ball (handball goalkeepers, soccer defenders) they had more time to simulate and diagnose. Rugby coaches, under less time pressure than athletes, used analytic decisions often.
numbers: Reported qualitatively, no new numbers in this piece.
quote: decision-making in a sport setting may take place on a continuum between intuitive and analytical processes
limits: The authors admit there is a lack of consistent empirical evidence for the continuum.
agent_relevance: Switch from fast to slow mode should depend on available time and situation familiarity, not be fixed.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: advances in the RPD model (first option rate)
finding: Prior work says expert athletes choose their preferred first option most of the time, which makes them look non-creative. Creative players show wider visual search and better first options (Roca 2018; Klatt 2019).
numbers: First option chosen in about 80% of decisions (as stated in this piece).
limits: The 80% is a secondary citation; the underlying primary source is not named in the passage.
agent_relevance: First-option commitment is the base rate in experts; an agent that always generates many options departs from expert behaviour.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: advances in the RPD model (six open questions)
finding: Names six gaps: interplay of intuition and analysis, visual search, creativity, emotion, development of intuition, team intuition. No sport study of emotion inside RPD existed to the authors' knowledge. Three hypotheses: affect guides matching; discomfort triggers more search; discomfort from a simulation prompts switching option.
numbers: Six research avenues; three emotion hypotheses; no data.
limits: Hypotheses only. Untested in sport as of 2022.
agent_relevance: Discomfort or a bad feeling as a trigger to leave fast mode maps to a confidence or anomaly trigger for the slow operator.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: advances in the RPD model (development of intuition)
finding: Development of intuition lacks sport evidence. Baylor (2001) proposed a U-shaped path: early immature intuition is high, drops as decisions become analytic, then rises. Training of intuitive decisions based on NDM has little empirical support.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Theoretical proposal, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Suggests a novice-like analytic phase is useful before reliable intuition; relevant for how the agent builds a case library.

source: Ashford, Abraham and Poolton (2021) Understanding a player's decision-making process in team sports: systematic review
finding: Systematic review of 53 empirical articles, 9 databases to March 2021. Compares three views: information processing, RPD, ecological dynamics. Concludes the role of mental representation depends on complexity, typicality, time available and contextual priors. Decisions lie on a continuum from emergent to top-down evaluation.
numbers: 53 articles; 36 studies on expertise characteristics; 21 characteristics grouped in perception, action capability, knowledge.
limits: Narrative synthesis, not a meta-analysis. Mostly small samples, many video or lab tasks.
agent_relevance: Gives the conditions that should decide which mode the agent uses: typicality, time, prior context, complexity.

source: Ashford, Abraham and Poolton (2021) Understanding a player's decision-making process in team sports: systematic review (RPD levels in team sport)
finding: Macquet (basketball, volleyball) found players rarely verbalised Level 3 evaluation by simulation. As typicality fell, players made more deliberate sense-making and risk assessment (Level 2). Ice hockey experts used patterns to judge typicality (Mulligan 2012); rugby league experts clustered cues and decided with little thought when typical (Johnston and Morrison).
numbers: Macquet volleyball n=7 professional men; Macquet and Kragba basketball n=7 elite women (from review table).
limits: Review summary of qualitative studies; very small n.
agent_relevance: Typicality judgement is the real switch. Simulation is seldom used even by experts in fast sport.

source: Ashford, Abraham and Poolton (2021) Understanding a player's decision-making process in team sports: systematic review (time manipulation, Basevitch)
finding: Video studies with expert coach rankings of options: experts beat near-experts. With less time, first intuitive responses were more accurate; with more time, generating more options was better. Musculus (2018) found only less-is-more support: fewer options went with accurate first response. Klatt: Brazilian players beat German players with both more options and a more accurate first option.
numbers: Time limits 400, 200 or 0 ms in Basevitch et al.
limits: Reported second-hand; the three primary papers were not opened. Mixed results across studies.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the best strategy flips with time budget. Supports a time or budget parameter on option generation.

source: Ashford, Abraham and Poolton (2021) Understanding a player's decision-making process in team sports: systematic review (visual search ambiguity)
finding: Eye-tracking data on experts are ambiguous; experts adapt search to task demands. Ecological-dynamics studies often use small decontextualised sub-phases (2v1 rugby, 1v1 basketball), which limits generality of their advice.
numbers: No pooled numbers.
limits: Authors flag method limits; criticism targets Correia et al. five rugby papers.
agent_relevance: Warns against generalising from narrow task slices; test the agent on varied situations.

source: Roca, Ford and Memmert (2018) Creative decision making and visual search behavior in skilled soccer players
finding: 44 skilled male soccer players watched life-size video of 11v11 attacks occluded at a key moment, played the ball, then listed other options for 45 s. Top 11 vs bottom 11 on creativity were compared with eye tracking. Most-creative produced more original, flexible and appropriate decisions.
numbers: N=44, groups n=11 each. Overall creativity t(20)=12.75, d=5.36; originality of first response d=2.12; fluency d=3.34; flexibility d=3.40.
limits: Extreme-group design (top vs bottom quarter) inflates effect sizes. Male English semi-pro and pro players only. Video, not live play.
agent_relevance: First-response quality and option breadth are separable skills; the agent could score them separately.

source: Roca, Ford and Memmert (2018) Creative decision making and visual search behavior in skilled soccer players (gaze)
finding: Creative players used more fixations of shorter duration and to more locations, and fixated attackers in threatening positions longer and earlier. This means broader attention gathered cues sooner.
numbers: Fixation duration d=1.24; fixations/s d=1.32; locations/s d=0.91. Time on threatening attacker 19.1% vs 10.7% (d=1.84). First threatening attacker found at 2164 ms vs 3798 ms (d=1.58). About 4 vs 3 threatening attackers per trial. Time on ball carrier overall 36.0%.
limits: Prediction made in advance; hypotheses matched results. Correlational. Does not show broad search causes creativity.
agent_relevance: Cue breadth early in the situation precedes better options; supports a wide cue scan step before commitment.

source: Le Menn, Bossard, Travassos, Duarte and Kermarrec (2019) Handball goalkeeper intuitive decision-making: a naturalistic case study
finding: One expert goalkeeper, self-confrontation interview over 26 shot sequences in an official match. 83 short accounts of decisions were coded into RPD levels. Simple match was most common but not as dominant as in older studies.
numbers: 83 accounts: simple match 38 (46%), simulation 28 (34%), diagnosis 17 (20%). 419 units of salient features: cues 185 (44%), expectancies 93 (22%), actions 74 (18%), knowledge 43 (10%), goals 16 (4%), consequences 8 (2%).
limits: N=1. Retrospective verbal report. Coding of RPD level from language register is subjective.
agent_relevance: Cue-heavy, goal-light content: experts report cues and expectancies far more than goals or consequences.

source: Le Menn, Bossard, Travassos, Duarte and Kermarrec (2019) Handball goalkeeper intuitive decision-making: a naturalistic case study (distance test)
finding: Distance to the thrower did not predict which RPD process was used, but it did predict the type of micro-decision. Mean distance for simple match 7.17 m, simulation 7.81 m, diagnosis 9.15 m.
numbers: Kruskal-Wallis for processes chi2(2)=1.044, p=0.593; for micro-decisions chi2(3)=26.53, p<0.001.
limits: Single participant; the small trend (more distance, more diagnosis) was not significant.
agent_relevance: A time-pressure proxy did not cleanly switch mode in this case; mode choice may depend on perceived familiarity more than raw time.

source: Le Menn, Bossard, Travassos, Duarte and Kermarrec (2019) Handball goalkeeper intuitive decision-making: a naturalistic case study (prior study rates)
finding: Reports older sport RPD results. Volleyball, soccer, ice hockey, Australian football: at least 80% simple match, about 15% diagnosis, under 5% simulation. Kermarrec and Bossard (2014) soccer defenders were the exception.
numbers: Kermarrec and Bossard 2014: 118 defending situations; simple match 60% (n=68), simulation 23% (n=26), diagnosis 16% (n=18).
limits: Second-hand numbers; the 2014 paper was not opened. These rates (80+ percent) differ from the 60-81% range quoted by Bossard 2022 for Macquet 2020 (different aggregation).
agent_relevance: Defenders with more time simulate more. Mode mix shifts with role and time, as the schema's operators would predict.

source: Collins, Collins and Carson (2016) If it feels right, do it: intuitive decision making in high-level sport coaches
finding: Interviews with 10 adventure-sport coaches and 8 rugby union coaches. Both groups reported high use of intuition, but rugby coaches rated it lower. Coaches often decided intuitively first, then checked deliberately, and rules emerged from reflection on intuitive actions.
numbers: n=10 adventure sports, n=8 rugby union. Rugby estimates of intuition averaged about 30% (range 5-40%). One adventure coach said about 90% intuitive.
limits: Self-estimated percentages; coaches had trouble giving them. Interview data, small n, post-hoc rationalisation noted.
agent_relevance: Pattern 'intuitive first, then deliberate check' is a two-pass design the agent can copy. Self-reports of share are unreliable.

source: Del Missier, Visentini and Mantyla (2015) Option generation in decision making: ideation beyond memory retrieval (cites Johnson and Raab 2003)
finding: Describes the Take The First result: handball players under time pressure generated options whose average quality fell as more were generated and as generation order advanced; more options led to less consistent, poorer choices (contrast: Ward et al., 2011).
numbers: Johnson and Raab (2003) numbers not given in this passage.
limits: Second-hand. The original paper was behind a paywall and was not opened.
agent_relevance: Strong support for first-option-first generation under tight time. Not a rule for all conditions.

source: Del Missier, Visentini and Mantyla (2015) Option generation in decision making: ideation beyond memory retrieval (own test of less-is-more)
finding: In three ill-structured option problems with 141 undergraduates and long time, fluency correlated negatively with mean option quality, so less-is-more appeared even without strict time limits. But more options also raised the best option's quality (quantity breeds quality). The effect varied by problem.
numbers: N=141, age M=22.7; fluency stability across problems r=0.46; quality-of-best option stability only r=0.17 (parking vs energy problems).
limits: Students on everyday problems, not athletes. Quality rated by trained raters, not experts. Authors suggest effect may be weaker in familiar domains.
agent_relevance: Both effects can coexist: sample few for mean quality, many for max quality. Agent should choose by objective.

source: Kalis, Kaiser and Mojzisch (2013) Why we should talk about option generation in decision-making research
finding: Notes Raab and colleagues work on option generation in sport, with options as fine-grained movement variants (velocity, release angle, spin). Claims option generation needs no elaborate processing, combining direct perception and bounded rationality. Memory retrieval plays a large role; effort depends on familiarity.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Conceptual paper.
agent_relevance: Option generation is a separate step in the loop, worth its own operator and budget.

source: Editorial (2023) Naturalistic decision making (NDM): epistemic expertise in action, Frontiers Research Topic
finding: Editorial of a 2023 Frontiers topic. One paper (Dorton et al.) argues NDM principles and tools suit the challenge of integrating AI into complex sociotechnical systems; another (Klein et al.) gives a plausibility transition model of sensemaking.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Editorial summary only; no sport content and no LLM test.
agent_relevance: Link to sensemaking subfield; shows NDM being applied to AI deployment, not tested on LLM reasoning.

source: Macquet (2009) Recognition within the decision-making process: a case study of expert volleyball players
finding: Founding sport RPD case study of expert volleyball players using self-confrontation interviews and the six-category coding (cues, goals, actions, expectancies, knowledge, consequences) later reused by Bossard, Kermarrec, Le Menn.
numbers: n=7 professional men (from Ashford 2021 table). Other numbers not read.
limits: Publisher page returned 403; not opened. Facts come from the opened Ashford and Le Menn papers.
agent_relevance: Six-category scheme can be adapted to code LLM traces.

source: Johnson and Raab (2003) Take The First: option-generation and resulting choices
finding: Founding option-generation study in handball: the first options generated are better, later ones worse, and considering more options hurt choice.
numbers: See Del Missier 2015 for the summary; exact sample and effect sizes not read.
limits: Paywalled, not opened.
agent_relevance: Origin of the take-the-first principle. Needs a primary read in a later pass.

source: Kermarrec and Bossard (2014) Defensive soccer players decision making: a naturalistic study
finding: 118 defending decisions of soccer players, RPD-coded. Higher simulation use than other sports, attributed to defenders having more time. Distance from the ball predicted taking time to diagnose or simulate.
numbers: Simple match 60% (n=68), simulation 23% (n=26), diagnosis 16% (n=18) as quoted in Le Menn 2019.
limits: Not opened; DOI not verified this session; quoted percentages sum to 99%.
agent_relevance: Mode mix depends on role.

source: Klatt and colleagues (2019) Creative and intuitive decision-making: Brazilian and German soccer coaches and players
finding: Two studies, coaches and players, video of real matches. Creativity score correlated positively with first-option quality across the whole sample. Brazilian players had more options and better first options than German players.
numbers: Effect sizes not read.
limits: Paywalled; author list unverified; facts from Bossard 2022 and Ashford 2021.
agent_relevance: Supports first-option quality as a skill that creative players also have.

source: Search for LLM or AI studies that test RPD in sport
finding: No LLM or AI study testing RPD or sport NDM was found with the arXiv, Europe PMC and Crossref queries that worked in this session. WebSearch budget was exhausted and OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned rate-limit errors, so this is a gap in coverage, not proof of absence.
numbers: 0 relevant hits in the Europe PMC and Crossref queries run.
limits: Search failure caveat. Retry later with budget.
agent_relevance: Treat LLM tests of sport RPD as unknown; use angle B or C results.
